newsitem.title: USA: Crop problems overseas may lift U.S. wheat exports.
newsitem.headline: Crop problems overseas may lift U.S. wheat exports.

text.p: Dry conditions in Australia and expected weak monsoons in India could hurt crops there and boost demand for U.S. wheat beyond the current U.S. Agriculture Department estimates, analysts said.
"I think we can easily bump up (exports) another 150 million bushels," said David Fiala, grain analyst at Alaron Trading Corp.
On Thursday, the USDA estimated 1997/98 (June/May) U.S. wheat exports at 1.025 billion bushels, up three percent from last year.
However, analysts said they expect USDA to gradually increase its wheat export number in subsequent reports.
Fiala said USDA probably would not raise the U.S. export estimate until later in the crop year, when production can be better estimated in the U.S. and overseas.
"It is a function of the supply around the world," said an analyst with a commercial grain firm. "Right today the (USDA's) demand numbers are just fine."
The analyst said should weather conditions hurt overseas crops then demand would likely increase for U.S. wheat.
An El Nino event in the south Pacific could extend already-dry conditions in Australia and could create similar conditions in Asia plus reduce rainfall in India's monsoons.
Canada also was expected to have a smaller wheat crop, with some farmers there switching acreage to oilseeds.

USDA estimated Canada's 1997 wheat harvest at 26 million tonnes, well below 30.5 million in 1996. USDA on Thursday raised Canada's wheat exports estimate to 19 million from 18 million a year ago, but some analysts said the export estimate appeared to be overstated.

USDA also estimated this year's Australian wheat crop at 18.5 million tonnes versus 23.59 million a year ago and also cut its Australia wheat export forecast to 14 million tonnes from 19 million a year ago.
The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics expects an even smaller crop. It said dry weather prompted by El Nino could cut that country's wheat harvest to 14 million tonnes.
Sid Love, analyst with Kropf/Love Consulting, said overseas crop problems could have USDA adding 100 million to 125 million bushels to U.S. wheat exports this year.
However, Love said he expects that to be partially offset by an upward revision in U.S. spring wheat output and reduction in wheat feed usage.

Love said USDA was estimating a U.S. spring wheat crop of about 700 million bushels, but he believes it will be closer to 750 million. Also, he said corn prices are low enough to discourage livestock producers from feeding large amounts of wheat.
USDA most recently estimated wheat feed and residual usage at 250 million bushels, but Love said that figure could later be cut to 175 million.
"The bottom line is...we could see a little larger (U.S.) spring wheat crop, reduced feed use and add some to exports," he said.

Assuming there are no additional problems with wheat crops in the U.S. and around the world, analysts said USDA's price forecast appears reasonable. In its Supply/Demand Report on Thursday, USDA indicated wheat prices of $3.45 to $4.05 per bushel in the 1997/98 crop year.
